Company of Heroes remains a landmark real-time strategy game because it approaches World War II combat as a constantly shifting tactical struggle rather than a straightforward contest of production and numbers. Developed and published by Relic Entertainment, it places squad positioning, territorial control, combined-arms tactics, environmental destruction, and unit preservation at the center of the experience. Its age is apparent in certain visual and interface elements, but the underlying mechanics remain remarkably engaging and continue to demonstrate why the game became so influential within the RTS genre.

The single-player campaign follows American forces beginning with the Normandy landings and continuing through battles across occupied Europe. Missions are designed around more than simply destroying every enemy unit on the map. Assaulting defensive positions, holding important locations, protecting forces, responding to counterattacks, and capturing strategically valuable territory create a campaign with considerable variety. The cinematic presentation gives major engagements a sense of scale without distracting from the tactical gameplay. Although the narrative is relatively straightforward, it provides enough context and personality to connect individual missions into a coherent military campaign.

Combat is where the game establishes its strongest identity. Infantry operates in squads, making each unit feel more valuable than the disposable soldiers found in many traditional strategy games. Cover plays a major role in survival, and positioning troops behind walls, inside structures, around wreckage, or within suitable terrain can dramatically improve their effectiveness. Charging across open ground toward a machine-gun position is usually disastrous, while suppression, flanking maneuvers, grenades, mortars, and coordinated attacks can dismantle the same defensive position. These systems reward players who study the battlefield before committing their forces.

The environment is more than visual scenery. Buildings can be occupied, damaged, and destroyed, while explosions and heavy weapons can transform areas that previously offered protection. Artillery can devastate fortified positions, tanks can smash through certain obstacles, and the remains of destroyed vehicles or structures contribute to the appearance of a battlefield that has genuinely experienced prolonged fighting. This destruction gives matches an organic quality because tactical opportunities can change as the terrain deteriorates.

Territorial resource management is another excellent element. Instead of focusing primarily on workers collecting resources from isolated deposits, players secure sectors scattered around the battlefield. Holding these locations provides the resources necessary to reinforce squads, construct units, purchase upgrades, and deploy heavier equipment. This encourages constant movement and prevents excessive defensive play. Capturing territory is important, but maintaining connections between controlled sectors can be equally significant, allowing aggressive players to disrupt an opponent's economy by cutting strategically important points.

The unit roster supports a strong combined-arms philosophy. Machine guns can suppress advancing infantry, but their limited firing direction makes them vulnerable to flanking. Mortars can attack entrenched enemies from a distance but require protection. Anti-tank weapons can threaten armored vehicles yet are vulnerable when caught by infantry. Tanks are extremely dangerous when properly supported, but careless commanders can lose expensive armor to mines, anti-tank guns, or coordinated attacks. Engineers, infantry squads, support weapons, artillery, and vehicles therefore work best as parts of a larger tactical force rather than as independent solutions to every problem.

Unit preservation also contributes greatly to the strategic depth. Experienced squads can become increasingly valuable, making retreating and reinforcing damaged units preferable to sacrificing them unnecessarily. The retreat system creates interesting decisions during difficult engagements because recognizing when a position has become impossible to hold can preserve important troops for a later counterattack. Losing territory temporarily is sometimes preferable to losing an entire veteran squad. This gives individual units a level of importance that makes victories and mistakes feel consequential.

Multiplayer takes the territorial warfare concept even further. Human opponents can exploit predictable defenses, cut supply routes, establish ambushes, and counter specific unit compositions more effectively than scripted opposition. Matches can develop into prolonged struggles where territory repeatedly changes hands and previously secure defensive positions are destroyed by artillery or armored assaults. The availability of community-created content and modification support also adds value for players interested in extending the experience beyond the standard campaign and multiplayer offerings.

Visually, the game naturally shows its age, particularly in character models, environmental detail, interface presentation, and some effects. Even so, the art direction maintains strong battlefield readability, and destruction continues to give combat impressive energy. Audio remains especially effective. Machine-gun bursts, artillery impacts, explosions, vehicle engines, unit dialogue, and distant fighting combine to create an intense atmosphere. Battles often sound chaotic without making important gameplay information impossible to recognize.

There are some frustrations. Pathfinding can occasionally cause infantry or vehicles to behave awkwardly, particularly in congested areas, while controlling multiple squads during large engagements can become demanding. Certain interface conventions also feel less refined by modern standards. New players may initially struggle with concepts such as suppression, directional weapons, connected territory, cover quality, reinforcement, veterancy, and the vulnerabilities of different vehicles. Once these systems become familiar, however, they form an exceptionally rewarding tactical framework.

Steam Deck users should consider the game playable rather than assume a completely optimized handheld experience. Compatibility information indicates that it can run on Steam Deck, but it should not be treated as equivalent to an official Steam Deck Verified designation. Its relatively straightforward mechanics make handheld play feasible, although occasional adjustments or minor interface inconveniences may be possible. Players specifically buying or installing games for Deck use should therefore expect functional compatibility rather than guaranteed console-like optimization.

Company of Heroes ultimately succeeds because virtually every major mechanic encourages active tactical thinking. Territory matters, positioning matters, retreating matters, and the destruction of the environment can completely reshape an engagement. Despite some aging technology and occasional control or pathfinding frustrations, its combination of dynamic warfare, squad management, strategic map control, and combined-arms combat remains exceptionally satisfying. It is an enduring RTS classic whose strongest ideas continue to hold up remarkably well.

Without doubt this is a quality game, a classic of the RTS genre, although it's more of a hybrid between a real RTS and a tactic game like Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines. 
Without doubt there are many aspects of COH to praise: like the very detailed graphics ( especially for it's release date ), the sound effects, the well made campain in which every mission is based on historic events, and the incredible realism and detail oriented game-play. 

So why the negative review? Simply because I didn't particulary enjoy it. There is a saying that goes: "if you played ping-pong for a long time you will not be able to master tennis properly, and the other way around". Because in tennis you swing with the upper arm, and in ping-pong you swing with the wrist and lower arm. 
As a veteran of the real time strategy genre ( I'm talking about real RTS like Warcraft, Starcraft, Red Alert, Age of Empires, Age of Mythologhy and so on and so forth....) I find this game to be incredibly different. The game-play principles of Company of Heroes are simply incompatible with the mechanics that are used in the aforementioned games.
So for me playing COH was not nearly as fun as playing those classic RTS games, for many reasons. 
1)	COH forces you to play with a very limited amount of troops. The dreaded and annoying population cap means you will have to chose carefully what units to train and what you do with them, you get punished for every single wrong decision and very often it means loading time. 
2)	This is a game that is easy to learn but very hard to master. If you truly want to enjoy it, you must become an expert of the game. If you want to become an expert, you must study every single unit of every faction: the strenghts, weaknesses and traits of every single unit. And...there is a lot of units. This game is basically like paper-rock-scissors. Every unit is strong against some other unit but weak against another specific unit. Also you need to study the placement of the units on the terrain/environment. The very same unit could be basically useless on open territory, and very effective if under cover. Often I would underestimate the critical importance of cover, or I thought I sent them to cover but I didn't. You must click precisely on the pixel where there is cover, or it won't count. 
3)	This game requires a ridiculous amount of micromanagement. An example is upgrading units. You have to buy the upgrade in the upgrade building, but then you have to upgrade every unit 1 by 1, and you can't do it anywhere on the map, but only when the unit is on your controlled territory. This means that often an average player would forget to upgrade the units, because in other RTS games you just have to buy the upgrades in the building, and they apply automatically to all current and future units you train. Another example: the average infantry units are relatively weak, their forte is when they throw grenades or sachel charges. You have to micromanage every unit to do so. Why not giving the player the chance to give a universal order: „throw grenades whenever possible?“ – or „use special ability whenever possible“-so you can concentrate on other tasks? Also it's a little ridiculous when you see 2 opposing infantry units that just stand there and shoot at each other for 1 minute. In other RTS games the killing is much faster and all happens smoother.  Ok, I understand that this game wanted to be as realistic as possible, but this is too much in my opinion – this is so over the top it's entertaining only to the die hard fans of the genre. 
4)	Let's face it, the campain is hard. Let's say 60% of the missions were ok, standard difficulty and entertaining (altough very hectic, withouth a second of rest), but 40% or 30% of the missions were BRUTAL. Truly brutal. And I played on the normal difficulty, so I don't dare to wonder how it is on hard and expert. You constantly lack manpower, fuel and munition, because they build up slowly. You have to conquer all those strategic points all over the map, but also you have to defend the ones you own, and you have to defend your base because the enemy constantly harasses you all over the map, all the time, and of course you have a very limited amount of units because of population cap. The AI enemy often spawns strange amounts of units simingly out of nowhere. Often I would wonder: „where the hell did this wave of tanks/infantry come from and how did the computer build it so fast?“. 
So, in order to complete those 30% of truly obnoxious missions, I had to consult you tube walkthrough, because let's face it, you can't complete missions the way you want it, you have to do the way the developers anticipated it. 
„Ahhhh, so I wasn't supposed to attack the strategic points on the left side? I needed to go on the right side  because the enemy has some devastating artillery there, and a hidden base where they create infantry and tanks from! And that's the only way to complete this?!. Time to restart the mission!.“
Multiplayer is dead because everybody moved on to COH2 and COH3.
To conclude, this is a quality game that went too far in being meticulous, resulting in some very annoying missions, but most of the missions were kinda fun, altough very challenging and frantic.

The Best Realtime Strategy Game Ever Made. Everything else either leads up to Company Of Heroes, or it's trying to play catch-up. Sorry Starcraft, ya ain't as good as CoH. Sorry Wargame, you're boring to look at and boring to play compared to CoH. Sorry Men of War 2, you're a cheap rip-off of CoH (and if I wanted to micromanage a per-unit, grid-based inventory, I'd play Diablo; that s**t sucks in a RTS).

Considering this game is now 14 years old at the time of this review, it should say a lot that there hasn't been a realtime strategy game that looks as good as CoH. Most of the environment is destructible, shells and bombs put different kinds of craters in the ground depending on how big the round is, and just about everything seems to have some kind of physics to it. Hit a group of infantry with an artillery round and watch as their body parts fly about, and even their rifles fly out of their hands and bounce on the ground. 

The sound effects and music are all top-notch as well. The voice acting is surprisingly good, and you'll hear familiar voices such as Spike from Cowboy Bebop, Garrus from Mass Effect, and many more. The things the units say range from badass to hilarious.

The gameplay is really, really good. There is a huge depth of strategy, thanks to the large number of units and commander abilities. The cover mechanic for infantry is excellent, and changes the dynamic of what an RTS even is. You can also use a special "retreat" command on infantry that lets them quickly run away and make it back to your headquarters so you can reinforce them, which you want to do since they level up as they get kills, and veteran infantry can become devastatingly powerful. Vehicles and actually all units also can level up too, making even the crappiest-seeming Jeep into something you actually want to keep alive. 

Once you master the vanilla game, there are many highly excellent mods, such as Blitzkrieg Mod, which greatly extend and enhance the game. If you like RTS games or strategy games in general, give Company of Heroes a shot. It's well worth it.

In my ongoing and likely futile effort to write a Steam review for every game in my library (#419 out of 612)... it's time for Company of Heroes.

The definitive WWII-era real-time tactical strategy game! Company of Heroes is one of the classics of the genre for good reason: it boasts and complex set of mechanics that make every combat encounter tense and engaging, and takes the player on a mostly-entertaining (if somewhat sanitized) romp through the theater of the Western Front in a campaign that does an excellent job bringing the history of the second world war to life.

Even today, Company of Heroes stands out as one of the finest tactical strategy games on the market, and will likely retain that position for many years to come—and not just for want of competition.

Company of Heroes remains one of the major landmarks in the real-time strategy genre and, alongside Homeworld, is certainly one of my favourite RTS games in history. The game strikes a fine balance between accessibility and depth, and even nearly 20 years on, it still feels solid, particularly in its cover, suppression, and environmental destruction systems. In my opinion, many RTS games that followed have struggled to replicate the same tactical feel. Even after all this time, it can still deliver intense battles without getting bogged down in bureaucracy.

Compared to Men of War, which focuses on meticulous micromanagement of soldiers and vehicles, Company of Heroes emphasises the rhythm of combat and the importance of positioning, with a brisk pace and a cinematic presentation that is almost caricatured, yet highly distinctive within the franchise. This contributes to the game feeling, in a sense, both accessible and remarkably current.

The soundtrack deserves special mention: epic, well-orchestrated, and always perfectly timed to heighten the tension and weight of each battle. It’s the kind of music that lingers in the memory and reinforces the atmosphere of total conflict. In this regard, the game truly does not disappoint, after all, in any experience striving for cinematic impact, the score is essential.

Even after all these years, Company of Heroes remains relevant and impresses both with the quality of its design and the strength of its presentation. One of Relic’s many great works, and an essential classic for any RTS enthusiast and fan of the Second World War.

The original Company of Heroes isn't just a classic; it’s a masterclass in game design that fundamentally changed how we think about real-time strategy. Before this game, most RTS titles were about gathering wood and gold to build a massive army. Relic Entertainment flipped that on its head, focusing instead on "territory control" and "tactical positioning." The result is a game that feels incredibly visceral and high-stakes. Every hedgerow, brick wall, and bombed-out building in Normandy matters. It turned the battlefield into a living, breathing puzzle where a single well-placed anti-tank gun or a daring flanking maneuver by a squad of paratroopers could turn the tide of an entire match.

Even decades later, the physics and destructibility in this game are more impressive than many modern titles. Seeing a Tiger tank crash through a stone wall or watching a mortar shell leave a permanent crater in the road isn't just visual flair—it’s a core part of the gameplay. The "Essence Engine" created a level of cinematic immersion that was unheard of in 2006, making every skirmish feel like a scene pulled straight out of Saving Private Ryan. The campaign, which follows Able Company through the liberation of Europe, remains one of the best-paced and most memorable narratives in the genre, serving as both a brilliant tutorial and a gripping war story.

While sequels have come and gone, there is a "purity" to the original Company of Heroes that keeps its community alive to this day. The balance between the factions—the versatile Americans and the defensive-heavy Wehrmacht—is legendary, leading to some of the most intense and competitive multiplayer matches in RTS history. It’s a game that demands your full attention; you can't just "blob" your units and hope for the best. You have to manage suppression, retreat at the right moment to save your veterans, and constantly adapt to a changing environment. It is a timeless masterpiece that every strategy fan needs to have in their library.

Anyone who has played Relic's most recent RTS hit Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War will understand the style of play here. The developers have simply improved on and adapted the rules of the previous game to fit the subject matter. Instead of simply grabbing generic resource points and constructing power generators, players will capture points (to raise their population cap and rate that manpower pours in), gather ammunition, and boost fuel supplies. Those three resources are what keep an army functioning. What's interesting is that the three resources can have pretty different applications: manpower is used in all unit and building construction, fuel is necessary to raise structures and purchase new vehicles, and ammunition is generally used to equip units with special weapons or activate special abilities on individual units like grenades or command tree abilities like air strikes. Maps often have larger amounts of certain types of resources making the way a mission progresses pretty unique.
Having three different capture points, all governing territories that are different shapes, creates a new level of strategy in all forms of the game. In order for one of these points to generate resources, it must be captured and connected back to the HQ territory via other friendly territories. If not, that resource is cut off and all benefits are denied. This gameplay mechanic comes into play more in skirmish and multiplayer, but does come into play in a few of the single player campaign missions.

The campaign in general is wonderfully designed and follows Able Company and Fox Company Paratroopers from the storming of Normandy to the defeat of the German 7th Army as Polish, Canadian, and US troops closed the Falaise Pocket. Fighting will take players from open roads and farming communities to the dangerous hedgerows of Hill 192 and tight city quarters of Cherbourg and St. Lo. Campaign missions are prefaced by excellent briefings that give a tiny history lesson and explain the situation using animatics and maps of France. Some striking in-engine cutscenes serve as bookends to most scenarios. The occasional mid-mission cut adds in extra detail. While usually unimportant to actual gameplay, they serve as exciting and rewarding intermissions mid-action.

Company of Heroes is a must-own title for every fan of the RTS genre. The campaign is excellent and allows you to play through some of the major engagements during the invasion of Normandy. The campaign naturally starts with the D-Day beach landing - you control Able company assigned to take Omaha beach. It then switches gears as you control some squads of the 101st Airborne, assigned to cut supply lines to the beachhead the night before the landings. From there the campaign takes you to well-known engagements in places like Carentan, Cherbourgh, St. Lo, and finally Chambois and the closing of the Falaise Pocket.

Gameplay mainly revolves around sector control, which is established by capturing, holding and optionally reinforcing a strategic point. A sector might simply be strategically valuable, but (depending on its type) may also provide you with necessary supply in the form of manpower, munitions and fuel. Manpower you'll need to field units, munitions for buying upgrades and using (unit) abilities and fuel for building structures, fielding vehicles and buying upgrades also. The enemy will require these supplies as well, so sector control can be a constant struggle as battle lines can shift rapidly. However, not all of these options are available in every mission, as you need control of a field HQ to build structures, which are in turn required to field (most) new units. For instance, the second mission, that you play as the 101st Airborne, has you capturing strategic points that grant manpower and munitions, but as you do not have a field HQ you can only use these supplies to reinforce existing squads and use their abilities, or airdrop new squads.
Combat is quite fun as concepts like cover, flanking and suppression play a major part. For instance, a squad of riflemen strolling down a road out of cover gets chewed up fast, especially by a heavy machine gun or an unlucky mortar strike. That same squad grabbing cover by a wall, or in a ditch, is much more resilient. Having that same squad take a heavy machine gun head on is suicide, as it will quickly be suppressed, rendered ineffective and killed. Flanking that same machine gun and tossing a grenade makes much more sense. A tank caught by a surprise attack from the side or even worse - the rear - is in serious danger, whereas its front armor can resist most attacks. You get the idea.

As someone who's horrible at RTS games, and therefor doesn't play them a whole lot; Company of Heroes is the one exception for me. It's just so damn good, even despite it's age. These two mechanics combined make every match, skirmish, & campaign mission feel fresh every time with adverse challenges & successes arising in different ways every game, writing a story of battle that you'll reflect on & learn from. The depth of Company of Heroes is so rewarding that even in the midst of a loss there's fun to be had.

 To top all that off, would be the map selection. Simply put, a masterpiece and one of my favourite games of all time.

Despite its original release 15 years ago, the mechanics, core game play, and nuanced strategy offered in the original Company of Heroes and its subsequent expansions are still unparalleled to date.

It is difficult to describe how satisfying it is to see your strategy work out in real time without actually experiencing it - your machine gun squad suppressing the pinned, helpless enemy riflemen, while your mortars and artillery reign down barrage after barrage. How your two pronged flanks completely take your enemy by surprise, and you laughing maniacally as the pathetic enemy shots bounce off the armour of your mighty tanks. Truly a feeling to remember. 

The game utilises physics and realism as well as any RTS I've played. Heavy tanks can easily clear out obstacles and walls, the importance of cover is heavily emphasised and often turns the tide of a troop engagement, garrisoned buildings crumble upon the impacts of heavy fire from cannons and much much more.

Although the online multiplayer is nowhere near as large as many other current games, finding a game is not a difficult. Yes, many of its players are quite seasoned, there are still a fair number of newbies who host and join matches to play against each other, or team up against the AI.

The campaign if all expansions are purchased, provides a wonderful experience. There are ~25 hours worth of game play in the missions alone, with plenty of variety along the way. Whether it's taking you to lead the Americans  on D Day, to managing a heroic German squad commanding a King Tiger tank, the missions are varied enough to provide constant entertainment.

The graphics have aged well in my opinion. You can zoom in to see the intricate details of each model and building. It does show its age in some areas, but overall, provides a great immersion while playing.

Plays much closer to Dawn of War, but I was hoping for something a bit more realistic. 

That's not to say this game isn't one of the best real time strategy games ever developed, its game-play formula is accessible and rewarding. If you aren't familiar with Relic's Dawn of War or its expansions, Company of Heroes follows a simple equation that consists of light base building using engineers and troop and vehicle generation through resources which include (manpower, munitions and fuel).  Using these resources, your engineers can build depots, establish a defensive perimeter in addition to building other structures and repairing vehicles. This just covers the base building mechanics.

There are a variety of infantry units at your disposal such as airborne, rangers and general infantry that can all be upgraded to use special squad based weapons such as BARs and recoil less rifles. Weapons can also be picked up in the field such as mortars, rocket launchers and 30 cal. machine guns. 

There is also a point system that can be used to drop in airborne infantry, deploy rangers, air drop artillery and supplies as well as conduct recon and bombing and strafing runs with air support. However, only some these will be available to you based on your preference for airborne, general infantry or armored units, perk categories that you will select at the beginning of each mission. 

Infantry fights in squads and you will never be able to spawn an army beyond the population limit. You're literally fighting with about a little less than a company sized element for most missions. Squads consist of six soldiers and are generally very effective against most light infantry, that is until you encounter a machine gun. If your squad is being suppressed than you're soldiers have very few options other than to retreat unless there is a vehicle with an mg that can disrupt the enemy's suppression. One of my issues with the game is that very rarely squad's will fire from cover and most often will jump out of cover to get into hand grenade range. However, with a squad armed with M1 Garands and BARs, I don't understand why these soldiers can't hit anything, especially from behind cover. Worse yet, there is no melee option that I know of for troops, and soldiers will be laying in prone shooting at the ankles of an enemy solider that's standing directly in front of them. Most fights I spam the grenade button more than I'd like to just to break up enemy squads so I can capture the next sector or resource point. 

And that's where the game becomes strikingly similar to Dawn of War, this whole game is based on resource management and procurement. Capturing point to point and watching the map turn blue is really the crux of the game and to be quite honest, its pretty fun.  While its not essential for you to capture points every mission, the resource management makes this essential to keeping the momentum going as you lose troops. 

The moment to moment game-play is a lot of fun and very accessible if you're looking for an easy RTS to get into and the destruction is just awesome. Buildings and vehicles explode and crumble from detonation charges from engineers, flak cannons and grenades and the firefights are loud. Sometimes the game's sound design, which is impeccable, can get overwhelming. 

I've played a little over twenty-hours of Company of Heroes and I'm definitely looking forward to playing the expansions and the sequel. On a sale, this is a must buy.
